I managed to prove the following theorem in Lean:

theorem eq_det_of_mul_of_scalar_pow_fin {n : ℕ} [NeZero n]
    (f : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℂ → ℂ)
    (H1 : ∀ A B, f (A * B) = f A * f B)
    (H2 : ∀ μ : ℂˣ, f (μ • 1) = μ ^ n) :
    ∀ A, f A = A.det

I.e., assuming only multiplicativity (homomorphism) on complex matrices and scalars:

(H1)f(AB)=f(A)f(B) ,(H2)f(μI)=μn\begin{alignat*}{2} (H1)\quad & f(AB) = f(A)f(B) \,,\\ (H2)\quad & f(\mu I) = \mu^n \end{alignat*}(H1)(H2)​f(AB)=f(A)f(B),f(μI)=μn​

and no other assumptions, the solution exists and is unique and equal to the determinant f(A)=det⁡Af(A) = \det Af(A)=detA. The proof just requires undergraduate linear algebra. The determinant can thus be defined using the two assumptions (H1) and (H2).

Is this result new? Worth adding to Mathlib?

I searched online and asked many people and so far everybody was surprised that this is true. Usually the determinant can be derived from the alternating multilinear form using the rows of the matrix, so in a sense it's basis dependent, so I like that derivation less as the assumptions seem rather arbitrary. The above seems simpler, assuming only elementary properties (H1) and (H2) on matrices (not rows), so the assumptions are more "intuitive" to me.

I am completely new to Lean, I derived the above by hand on paper, but wasn't 100% sure I didn't make a mistake somewhere. I now formalized it in Lean (with the help of AI), and it works, which is amazing.
This is the characterization of determinant, it is the unique alternating map that takes f : K^n -> K such that f I = 1.
Above I am not assuming it is alternating.

Can you try rewriting it using LinearMap instead of Matrix Then what you have is f is a MulHom, in fact, a MonoidHom of linear maps. And H2 is just the statement H1 specialized to A = ((mu, 0, 0, ...), (0, 1, 0, ...),) (mu at one place on the diagonal of I, B = I`, done N times. Is that right?

MSE ref: https://math.stackexchange.com/a/1159921

Yes, using (H1) alone plus assuming measurability (which implies continuity), we can prove f=(sign(det⁡A))ε⋅∣det⁡A∣rf=(sign(\det A))^ε⋅|\det A|^rf=(sign(detA))ε⋅∣detA∣r (as in the link you sent), I have that formalized in Lean too. Then the determinant is the case ε=r=1ε=r=1ε=r=1, so you need some way to select it, one way is to assume (H2) above (which doesn't even require to assume any regularity), but it's not the only way. You are right that (H1) is the main assumption that provides a full classification of all solutions, and (H2) just selects the one we want.

Btw, the other values of ε and r correspond to different scalar densities, and it provides a nice classification of them --- it's not mentioned at all in the wikipedia entry. That's a whole another subject, but also new I think!

P.S. Thanks for the MSE link, I missed that one in my search. I know there are mentions of this property in abstract algebra on groups or even Lie groups. So it's not new, but from the proof at MSE (and elsewhere) it's not clear that you can prove this using just linear algebra, that you don't need more advanced group theory, and also it wasn't clear to me when doing it on paper that I don't use circular reasoning: using a determinant to build more advanced theory (groups, differential forms, etc.), and then using the advanced theory to "define" the determinant. I think formalizing in Lean prevents this pitfall.

I don't think in mathlib, one can even discuss det without a lot of "advanced theory" -- I think some of our proofs of its properties are done via raising to the polynomial ring: src#Matrix.det_adjugate
The argument in the MSE answer showing SLn(K)⊆NSL_n(\mathbb{K})\subseteq NSLn​(K)⊆N can also be replaced by this: since the codomain is abelian, the kernel must contain the commutator subgroup.

@Junyan Xu, yes, I've seen this derivation using groups, so I think this is must be a well-known result if you know groups/algebra.

@Yakov Pechersky: that's a good example: the theorem itself theorem det_adjugate (A : Matrix n n α) : (adjugate A).det = A.det ^ (Fintype.card n - 1) doesn't use polynomial rings, but the proof does. This is analogous to the eq_det_of_mul_of_scalar_pow_fin theorem above: I actually have two proofs, one using Mathlib (which inside might depend on determinants) and another more elementary, I was careful to derive everything myself, not to use many things from Mathlib, to avoid the dependency on determinants.

Question: if Lean's theorem about determinants (such as the one above) doesn't use Mathlib's determinants in the assumptions nor results, but the proof does, and Lean compiles it without errors, then does that guarantee that there is no circular dependency? That everything is built strictly by "adding" new theorems on top of already proven theorems?

As a specific example, let's say you use the det_adjugate theorem (whose proof uses polynomial rings) inside Mathlib's polynomial rings to prove some things there --- will Lean always 100% prevent you from any circular dependencies?

If so, then I think there is no problem in using "advanced theory" to prove "simple" theorems.
Circular dependencies are impossible in normal use because Lean theorems can't be used until they are in the environment and are put into the environment sequentially.

(there is a special mutual block which gives the illusion of locally disabling this behavior, but you as the user have to prove that your circular reasoning is sufficient legal for the elaborate to unwind it into something sequential behind the scenes)

Ondřej Čertík said:

If so, then I think there is no problem in using "advanced theory" to prove "simple" theorems.

This can matter if:

  • It results in a less strong theorem (one that holds less generally)
  • It substantially increases the "longest pole" compile time of mathlib
  • It increases the chance of accidentally creating circular imports while trying to modify a proof (which then forces the contributor to waste time moving a bunch of theorems around)

Thanks for confirming, this is great. Yes, it matters from the practical engineering perspective, but not from the "mathematical" perspective. The determinant is a great example of this, it's such a fundamental concept that when I use some more advanced theory by hand to "define" a determinant, I don't know how to ensure by hand I didn't accidentally use circular reasoning. But with Lean we can be sure.

Also I think this is related to using AI for the proofs: I think it doesn't matter from the "mathematical" perspective how ugly or long or verbose/complex the proof is, as long as Lean compiles it, I know the theorem is true. It only matters from the engineering perspective (so it greatly matters to me, of course).

I am absolutely amazed at the engineering capability of Lean and Mathlib. Totally usable now for most math used in physics for example. For example I have this book: https://www.theoretical-physics.com/dev/index.html with contains most of the fundamental physics (obviously only to a certain depth), and I have a large math section that derives ab-initio all the math needed in the book. I think it can be formalized in Lean now. I really like "simple" (I know it's subjective) derivations of math (and physics too) and so sometimes I derive things in a slightly unusual way, such as the determinant above from just homomorphism/homogeneity, not using the usual alternating map, but it's really easy to fool myself with circular reasoning. But now with Lean I can ensure everything is rock solid, logically building in layers on top of each other.

Also a lot of people asked me to use SymPy in the book, to make the equations "computable". But it's hard in practice, it's not a perfect fit. I feel Lean provides another piece in the puzzle, I think it might just work for most of the math section.
